parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving fire, smoke, injury, property damage, or emergency-service response to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a complete incident report within 10 business days. Other confirmed thermal incidents must be reported to the regulator within 5 business days. S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving fire, smoke, injury, property damage, or emergency-service response to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a complete incident report within 10 business days. Other confirmed thermal incidents must be reported to the regulator within 5 business days. The manufacturer must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident presents a credible safety risk or requires customer action, and provide updates as material information becomes available.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving fire, smoke, injury, property damage, or emergency-service response to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a complete incident report within 10 business days. Other confirmed thermal incidents must be reported to the regulator within 5 business days. The manufacturer must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident presents a credible safety risk or requires customer action, and provide updates as material information becomes available. Reports must include known incident counts and installed-unit denominators; corrected or previously omitted reports must be promptly submitted.

parameters.quote: Manufacturers must provide per-model sample sizes, failure rates, and supporting test results to the relevant regulator at certification and after each retest, and must provide the model's failure rate and material supporting test results to prospective customers before purchase. A failure rate above 5% exceeds the performance criterion and requires prompt notice to regulators, a corrective-action plan, and retesting under the approved protocol. Regulators may require additional safeguards or restrict sales based on the risk and adequacy of remediation; exceeding 5% alone does not automatically prohibit certification or continued sale.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Manufacturers must provide per-model sample sizes, failure rates, and supporting test results to the relevant regulator at certification and after each retest, and must provide the model's failure rate and material supporting test results to prospective customers before purchase. A failure rate above 5% exceeds the performance criterion and requires prompt notice to regulators, a corrective-action plan, and retesting under the approved protocol. Regulators may require additional safeguards or restrict sales based on the risk and adequacy of remediation; exceeding 5% alone does not automatically prohibit certification or continued sale.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before initial certification and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. Manufacturers must provide per-model sample sizes, failure rates, and supporting test results to the relevant regulator at certification and after each retest, and must provide the model’s failure rate and material supporting test results to prospective customers before purchase. A failure rate above 5% exceeds the performance criterion and requires prompt notice to regulators, a corrective-action plan, and retesting under the approved protocol. Regulators may require additional safeguards or restrict sales based on the risk and adequacy of remediation; exceeding 5% alone does not automatically prohibit certification or continued sale. Per-model results must not be published to the general public.

parameters.quote: New home battery systems placed on the market must include a remotely operable emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a documented means for customers or emergency responders to request activation. For units installed before this requirement takes effect, manufacturers must offer a compatible retrofit or equivalent mitigation within 6 years, prioritizing units with known safety concerns and notifying affected owners of available options.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New home battery systems placed on the market must include a remotely operable emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a documented means for customers or emergency responders to request activation. For units installed before this requirement takes effect, manufacturers must offer a compatible retrofit or equivalent mitigation within 6 years, prioritizing units with known safety concerns and notifying affected owners of available options.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New home battery systems placed on the market must include a remotely operable emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a documented means for customers or emergency responders to request activation. Manufacturers must provide software and communications support for the function. For units installed before this requirement takes effect, manufacturers must offer a compatible retrofit or equivalent mitigation within 6 years, prioritizing units with known safety concerns and notifying affected owners of available options.

parameters.quote: New home battery systems placed on the market must include built-in fire suppression. This requirement takes effect 36 months after adoption of this standard.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New home battery systems placed on the market must include built-in fire suppression. This requirement takes effect 36 months after adoption of this standard.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New home battery systems placed on the market must include built-in fire suppression. This requirement takes effect 36 months after adoption of this standard. Manufacturers must provide regulators with evidence of compliance as part of model certification.

parameters.quote: A manufacturer must initiate a regulator-supervised recall when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any 12-month period. Manufacturers must promptly notify owners of newly identified material safety risks, recommended precautions, and corrective actions, and provide updates as material information becomes available.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: A manufacturer must initiate a regulator-supervised recall when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any 12-month period. Manufacturers must promptly notify owners of newly identified material safety risks, recommended precautions, and corrective actions, and provide updates as material information becomes available.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Before purchase, customers must receive clear safety information for the specific model, including its 55 °C sustained-heat test results and relevant incident and recall notices. Manufacturers must promptly notify owners of newly identified material safety risks, recommended precautions, and corrective actions, and provide updates as material information becomes available. A manufacturer must initiate a regulator-supervised recall when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any 12-month period. Manufacturers must report model-level incident counts and installed-unit denominators to regulators and affected customers, and notify customers promptly when the recall threshold is met.

I’ve revised S2 to preserve 5% as a meaningful regulator-action benchmark while avoiding automatic market exclusion. The verified Hearth 10 rate is 6.2%, so an automatic sales bar would have an immediate and disproportionate effect; regulator oversight, corrective action, retesting, and risk-based safeguards provide a path to address safety without treating the benchmark as an automatic ban.
